title: Growing up
subtitle: a toddler, in your teens, brought up
summary: Name the stages of life from birth to old age, give someone's age approximately, and talk about how you were brought up.

lesson.heading: Ages and stages in the UK
rows: **birth** - the moment a baby is born
a **teenager**; during this period you are **in your teens**
people are **middle-aged** - in the middle of their lives
**retirement**, when people stop work; they are **retired**
**old age**; we usually describe people as **elderly**

lesson.heading: Approximate ages
lesson.text: When you do not know someone's exact age, use **early**, **mid-** or **late** with the decade, or say **nearly**, **almost**, **approximately** or **roughly**.

examples.text: My grandmother is in her **late seventies**.

examples.note: = he's probably 79; almost means the same

lesson.text: Say *he's 30* or *he's 30 years old*, not ~~he has 30~~ or ~~he's 30 years~~. And say *a 30-year-old man*, not ~~a 30-years-old man~~.

lesson.heading: My grandmother's childhood
lesson.text: A young woman talks about her grandmother Mary, who is now **dead** (the opposite is **alive**). She died about ten years ago. Mary was **brought up** on a farm in Wales, which means her parents looked after her there until she was an adult.

examples.text: She's **dead** now. She died when I was in my teens.
examples.note: dead = not living; the opposite is alive

examples.text: She was **brought up** on a farm in Wales.
examples.note: bring someone up = look after them until they are an adult
strict = they made her obey a lot of rules

examples.text: They didn't **allow** her to listen to the radio or go to parties.

lesson.heading: Leaving home
lesson.text: **In the end** means finally, after a lot of time or thought. **At first** means at the beginning. If you **manage** to do something, you are able to do it, but it is difficult.

examples.text: **In the end**, she decided to leave home and get a job in Cardiff.
**At first** it wasn't easy, but she **managed** to find work.
She met the man who became her husband. My mother was **born** four years later.
My mother **grew up** in the city and had a very different **childhood**.

lesson.heading: let and allow

left.label: let (more informal)
examples: My dad **let** me drive his car.
Her parents **let** her stay out late.

right.label: allow (often passive)
examples: I **was allowed to** drive my dad's car.
She **wasn't allowed to** listen to the radio.
You're **not allowed to** smoke in that room.

lesson.note: Say *You're not allowed to smoke in that room*, not ~~It's not allowed to smoke in that room~~.

exercises.prompt: Isabella is only six months old - she's still a ___.
exercises.explanation: A child up to 12 months old is a baby.

exercises.prompt: Holly is just over a year old and she's starting to walk, so she's a ___ now.
exercises.explanation: A child between about 12 months and three years is a toddler.

exercises.prompt: Abigail will be 13 this year, so she'll soon be a ___.
exercises.explanation: From about 13 to 18 you are a teenager.

exercises.prompt: Louis was 22 a few months ago, so he's in his ___.
Amelia is 35. How do we describe her age?
William is 53 and his wife is 47, so they're both ___.
exercises.explanation: People of about 40 and over are middle-aged.

exercises.prompt: Put each word in the right stage of life.

exercises.statement: Mary was brought up in the city.
exercises.explanation: Mary was brought up on a farm in Wales.

exercises.statement: Mary's parents let her do what she wanted.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence with the sentence that means the same.

pairs.left: It was hard, but finally I did it.
pairs.right: It was hard, but in the end I did it.

pairs.left: My mum looked after me in Scotland.
pairs.right: I was brought up in Scotland.

pairs.left: My grandparents don't work any more.

exercises.prompt: I was able to pass my exams, but it wasn't easy. I ___ to pass my exams.
exercises.explanation: manage to do something = be able to do it, but with difficulty.

exercises.prompt: My parents let me wear what I liked, so I was ___ wear what I liked.
exercises.explanation: let someone do something = allow someone to do something. Allow needs to.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to say what Mary's strict parents did not permit.
exercises.answer: She wasn't allowed to listen to the radio.
exercises.explanation: Allow is often used in the passive: be allowed to do something.
